articles.title: How AI is De-Risking Drug Development and Companion Diagnostics
articles.text:
Skip to main content Opinion How AI is De-Risking Drug Development and Companion Diagnostics Digital pathology and artificial intelligence are transforming the drug development landscape, accelerating the path to personalized medicine and better health outcomes. Written by Karan Arora Karan Arora Karan Arora is the Senior Vice President of Advanced Assays, AI, and Pharma Services at Leica Biosystems. View Full Profile Learn about our Editorial Policies . and Luiza Moore, MD, PhD Luiza Moore, MD, PhD Luiza Moore, MD, PhD, FRCPath is the Global Commercial Product Leader – AI Enabled Assays, at Leica Biosystems. View Full Profile Learn about our Editorial Policies . May 12, 2026 | 7 min read Save for Later Companion diagnostics enable more precise trials, faster development cycles, and better health outcomes for some of the world’s sickest patients. Image credit: © iStock.com, Yuuji PDF version Register for free to listen to this article Listen with Speechify 0:00 7:00 Share T he path to bringing a new drug to market is increasingly complex and costly, with development costs now exceeding $2 billion and timelines approaching a decade. 1,2 The stakes have never been higher—demanding new models, new technologies, and new thinking to reduce risk and accelerate breakthroughs. Up to 90 percent of compounds entering clinical trials never reach the market, often due to unforeseen toxicity or lack of efficacy in heterogenous patient populations. This high failure rate has accelerated a shift toward more targeted development strategies. Companion diagnostics are central to this shift, enabling more precise trials, faster development cycles, and better health outcomes for some of the world’s sickest patients. Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the landscape—not only for therapeutics but also for precision diagnostics that guide patient selection and treatment decisions. Digital pathology and AI now sit at the heart of this transformation, offering new ways to extract quantitative biological signals, harmonize global lab variability, and support earlier, sharper decision‑making in clinical trials. 3 From Failure to Focus: Reducing Drug Development Risk with Computational Pathology Biology is heterogeneous, traditional pathology is variable, and global clinical trial operations introduce noise that can obscure early efficacy or safety signals. 4 Whole‑slide imaging (WSI) and computational pathology have the potential to directly address these challenges by scaling objective readouts from tissue and associated morphology with clinical outcomes. Continue reading below... Like this story? Sign up for FREE Cancer updates: Latest science news stories Topic-tailored resources and events Customized newsletter content Subscribe With over 15 years of experience in diagnostics and pathology, I have seen how “identical” hematoxylin & eosin (H&E) slides can vary across sites—introducing noise, repeat reviews, and delayed decisions. This becomes particularly challenging when variability forces the tissue journey to restart, or worse, necessitates repeat tissue collection from patients, many of whom are critically ill—consuming precious, often irreplaceable patient samples and driving additional trial costs. AI‑enabled tissue quantification has the potential to address these challenges by reducing subjectivity, delivering more reproducible endpoints, and generating cleaner data earlier in drug development. AI can also serve as a second set of eyes during review, helping ensure critical features are not missed and increasing confidence in study outcomes. From Slides to Quantitative Biomarkers Modern AI models are capable of identifying subtle morphologic patterns that correlate with prognosis, molecular status, and treatment response. For example, multiple‑instance learning (MIL)-based approaches have matured to clinical‑grade performance for predicting histology-derived endpoints, providing objective, reproducible metrics appropriate for global deployment and regulatory evaluation. 5 These biomarkers further reduce biological uncertainty by enabling earlier biological signal detection and quantitative features that can be deployed consistently across global trials. This shift allows development teams to detect trends long before traditional clinical endpoints mature. 6 Strengthening Oncology Trial Decisions Through Early AI‑Enabled Signal Detection AI‑enabled biomarkers support early patient stratification, reduce biological and operational noise, and enable more accurate response prediction across oncology trials . Increasingly, studies demonstrate that morphology‑derived signatures extracted from routine histology can predict outcomes and drug response earlier—and often more reproducibly—than traditional clinical readouts. 6 This is particularly relevant in immuno‑oncology, where response to therapy is shaped by both tumor-intrinsic features and the tumor microenvironment. While established biomarkers such as PD‑L1 immunohistochemistry have been central to patient selection, they only capture part of this biological complexity. In this context, weakly supervised AI models applied to standard H&E sections can infer tumor microenvironment characteristics and immunotherapy response at scale, complementing PD-L1 based strategies and enabling earlier enrichment and informed decisions for treatment optimization. 3,6 Bridging the R&D–to–Real‑World Gap in CDx Development Companion diagnostics (CDx) failures often occur not during discovery, but at deployment—when real‑world laboratory variability undermines analytical performance. Multi‑center datasets consistently demonstrate significant inter-laboratory variation in staining and scanning, driving domain shift and degrading model performance unless proactively managed. 7 Recent studies underscore how stain‑normalization techniques are evolving to address this challenge. Methods such as Macenko, Reinhard, and Vahadane continue to serve as strong and reliable baselines, sustaining their role as workhorses in digital pathology workflows. In parallel, generative adversarial network‑based and hybrid approaches are demonstrating clear advantages in cross‑site robustness, enabling models to generalize more effectively across heterogeneous scanners and staining protocols. Most notably, techniques, such as stain‑aware normalization and Beer–Lambert-based models, offer substantial reductions in performance loss under shifting staining conditions, representing a meaningful advance toward more resilient and deployment‑ready image analysis pipelines. These capabilities are critical for achieving analytically valid CDx deployment across global laboratory networks. 8 Infrastructure Readiness: Cloud‑Native, Compliant, and Audit‑Ready Digital pathology infrastructure continues to mature globally, with cloud‑native, compliant, and fully auditable platforms emerging as the foundation for scalable deployment. The FDA clearance of WSI for primary diagnosis has further facilitated adoption, enabling clinical‑grade digital pathology infrastructure to operate reliably and securely across institutions. Importantly, the infrastructure readiness in AI-enabled pathology extends beyond software and cloud architecture to the full end-to-end system, from tissue handling to computational analysis. At present, glass slides remain the biological ground truth, supporting regulatory review, retrospective analysis, and future biomarker discovery. Not all whole-slide scanners are equivalent in optical quality, color fidelity, throughput, or reproducibility. These differences can have a significant impact on downstream algorithm performance if not carefully controlled. As AI-derived endpoints move into registrational trials and companion diagnostic deployment, the selection of clinically validated, high-performance scanning platforms become a critical component of infrastructure readiness. In parallel, regulatory expectations for AI in healthcare are becoming increasingly well defined, with greater emphasis on adherence to Good Machine Learning Practice (GMLP), transparency in AI‑generated outputs, and robust oversight across the total product lifecycle—including proactive post‑market monitoring.  For AI-enabled assays, this includes controls such as cell line and reference material controls, locked models, cross-lab performance monitoring, and auditable data lineage. Cloud‑native pipelines, designed to meet HIPAA/GDPR requirements, can now offer essential capabilities such as comprehensive audit trails, encryption, role‑based access control, and data lineage. Together, these developments support deployment-ready, regulator-aligned digital pathology workflows for next-generation companion diagnostics and clinical decision support. Regional CDx Regulatory Landscape In the US, the FDA provides relatively clear CDx co‑development pathways , supported by oncology‑focused pilot programs that encourage early alignment between therapeutic and diagnostic development. In Europe, the In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation (IVDR) elevates CDx to Class C, requiring Notified Body review and consultation with the European Medicines Agency . While this shift strengthens regulatory rigor and oversight, it also introduces increased workload, operational complexity, and longer development timelines. Comparative analyses show widening differences between FDA and IVDR requirements—underscoring the importance of coordinated, early regulatory planning. Without proactive alignment, these regional differences can introduce delays, rework, and downstream risk to global CDx deployment. AI Augmenting Pathologists Workflows AI has the potential to improve diagnostic accuracy, standardization, and efficiency in pathology. However, contextual interpretation, clinical judgement, and patient‑impacting decisions remain firmly within the expertise of the pathologist. Reviews continue to emphasize that safe and effective use of AI requires clinician‑in‑the‑loop workflows, where human oversight is integral to decision‑making. 9,10 As a cyto- and histopathologist, I have spent countless hours performing manual, time‑intensive tasks such as accurately counting inflammatory cells to diagnose acute bladder inflammation or enumerating mitotic figures to determine breast cancer grade, decisions that directly influence patient treatment. AI has the potential to relieve pathologists of these repetitive, low-value tasks, allowing us to focus on integrative reasoning, clinical context, and complex diagnostic synthesis—capabilities that algorithms cannot replicate. The Future: Multimodal, Generalizable, and Equitable Next‑generation multimodal foundation models integrate histology with clinical reports, genomics, and proteomics to improve disease classification, survival prediction, and biological interpretability across cancer types. These models move beyond single‑modality analysis, enabling richer context and more biologically meaningful insights. 8 When rigorously validated across sites and paired with stain‑robust deployment‑ready pipelines, these systems have the potential to expand access to precision diagnostics globally, including in low‑resource settings where specialist expertise and advanced infrastructure may be limited. 3,11 Importantly, AI is not a substitute for skilled laboratory staff and researchers; rather it serves as a powerful second set of eyes—enhancing precision, increasing agility, and elevating the quality of scientific work with deeper insights. Collaboration Delivers Greater Value In an environment where accelerating time‑to‑market is increasingly critical, building diagnostics capabilities from scratch can introduce unnecessary cost, delay, and execution risk. Strategic collaboration offers a more efficient path forward, allowing innovation to scale without sacrificing rigor or speed. Beyond operational efficiency, collaboration also enables a departure from traditional CDx partnership models that often constrain speed and flexibility. Emerging platform-based, data-centric approaches allow therapeutic and diagnostic development to progress in parallel, reducing hand-offs, compressing timelines, and enabling faster launches. Importantly, these models support earlier alignment on evidence generation, regulatory strategy, and global deployment—reducing late-stage friction that has historically delayed market entry. Partnerships are helping build comprehensive antibody libraries, powered by sophisticated AI analysis. Instead of starting anew, pharmaceutical companies can leverage robust, pre‑validated datasets to establish proof‑of‑concept more rapidly and with greater confidence. For emerging biomarkers, the platform’s ability to generate custom antibodies on demand adds critical flexibility and speed. Looking Ahead: A New Model for Evidence Generation As personalized medicine becomes the standard of care, the pressure on pharmaceutical companies to develop robust companion diagnostics has never been greater—elevating risk mitigation capabilities from operational considerations to sources of competitive advantage. AI is emerging as the new scientific lens for drug development and CDx. By reducing biological uncertainty, harmonizing variability across global laboratory networks, and supporting earlier, more confident decision‑making, AI is accelerating the path from discovery to meaningful patient impact. Critically, the next evolution of evidence generation will integrate real-world evidence (RWE) with clinical trial data. When combined with AI-enabled diagnostics, RWE enables ongoing validation of biomarker performance across more diverse patient populations, strengthening confidence in clinical utility beyond controlled trials. This approach allows best practices to be scaled more rapidly, accelerating the translation of approved innovations into meaningful patient impact. As cloud‑based pathology infrastructure continues to mature and regulatory frameworks for AI diagnostics evolve, these technologies will increasingly define how evidence is generated, validated, and translated into the next generation of precision therapeutics. Apr 20, 2026 | 3 min read Save for Later An oral cancer vaccine containing non-pathogenic Listeria paired with immune checkpoint inhibitors could lead to a new way to treat colon cancer. Image credit: ©iStock.com, FalconScallagrim PDF version Share I mmunotherapies have dramatically improved outcomes for patients with cancer, but some patient populations, such as a large subset of individuals with colorectal cancer, respond poorly to these treatments. However, a potential way to boost these therapies lies with an unexpected source: the foodborne pathogen Listeria monocytogenes . In a new study in mice, researchers found that ingestion of attenuated L. monocytogenes as an oral cancer vaccine elicited a cytotoxic T cell response in the gut and transiently halted colorectal tumor growth. 1 Co-administration of immune checkpoint inhibitors sustained this effect, highlighting a potential new path to harnessing the immune system against these deadly cancers. An Oral Vaccine Route for a Foodborne Pathogen-Based Therapy Prior L. monocytogenes -based vaccines were delivered intravenously to help them bypass the body’s natural defenses, but this route can lead to sepsis on rare occasions since the bacteria get delivered directly into the bloodstream. 2 The oral vaccine route, on the other hand, impressed Laurence Wood , an immunologist at Texas Tech University who was not involved in the study and who had previously developed an intravenous L. monocytogenes -based vaccine. 3 “The natural route of infection for Listeria is foodborne, so it makes sense to leverage that aspect of it,” Wood said. “I think it’s promising that it looks like work is going in this way.” Continue reading below... Sign up for FREE Cancer updates: Latest science news stories Topic-tailored resources and events Customized newsletter content Subscribe Study coauthor Semir Beyaz , a cancer biologist at Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory, added, “We think that it’s safer than what’s currently being used in clinical trials for Listeria. ” Researchers develop cancer vaccines using L. monocytogenes because the bacteria contain the protein internalin A, which binds to human E-cadherin, a protein that is often upregulated in tumors. 4 This allows L. monocytogenes to invade the cancer cells, and the bacteria’s presence calls immune cells to previously poorly immunogenic tumors. To test an L. monocytogenes -based vaccine in mice, the researchers first mutated it so that it could interact with the mouse E-cadherin protein. They then inoculated a piece of bread with the unattenuated bacteria and fed it to mice. For comparison, the researchers also administered L. monocytogenes to the animals intravenously. Oral administration of L. monocytogenes induced T cells to take up residence in the intestinal mucosa significantly more than when the bacteria were delivered intravenously. Residency is an important characteristic for conferring rapid immune response in the organ. The population of resident T cells remained high over three months after infection, demonstrating that orally administered L. monocytogenes could indeed produce a robust immune response. To make the vaccine safe, the team deleted genes associated with L. monocytogenes pathogenicity. The number of attenuated bacteria in the mouse intestine was comparable to the bacteria’s unattenuated counterparts. However, attenuated L. monocytogenes was hardly detectable in other organs, such as the spleen and liver, demonstrating that the bacteria stayed local and within the target organ, which suggested a lower risk for sepsis. Like their unattenuated counterparts, attenuated L. monocytogenes also induced T cell residency in the intestinal mucosa. Altogether, these results suggest that the vaccine with attenuated bacteria is safe in mice. A Listeria -Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Combo Targets Colon Cancer Next, the researchers evaluated the oral vaccine’s impact on cancer. The team implanted a mouse colon cancer cell line into the colon’s lining 10 days after immunization with attenuated L. monocytogenes . Nearly all the vaccinated mice's tumors shrank within a week after they were immunized. This contrasted with their sham-immunized counterparts, whose tumors grew significantly in that period. The researchers also tested the vaccine’s therapeutic potential. To do this, they immunized the animals a week before transplanting tumor organoids into their colons. Similarly, this approach considerably halted tumor growth compared to the control groups, but the suppression didn’t last and hardly improved survival. The team hypothesized that the activated T cells might have activated immune checkpoints, which in turn, dampened the resulting immune response. So, starting five days after immunization, the researchers also treated the mice with immune checkpoint inhibitors every other day for two weeks. Compared with either the vaccine or inhibitor treatment alone, the combination therapy significantly suppressed mouse tumor growth for nearly 40 days. Continue reading below... He didn’t think it would be a good idea to have people eat Listeria -contaminated food even if the bacteria were attenuated. To him, the approach the researchers used “doesn’t seem like it’s easily translatable.” Wood added, “I wouldn’t give it in bread because then you’re getting it also in your mouth,” suggesting more traditional oral formulation such as capsules. Written by Andrea Lius, PhD Andrea Lius, PhD Andrea Lius is a freelance science writer. She is working on her PhD in pharmacology at the University of Washington in Seattle. View Full Profile Learn about our Editorial Policies . Apr 20, 2026 | 3 min read Save for Later An oral cancer vaccine containing non-pathogenic Listeria paired with immune checkpoint inhibitors could lead to a new way to treat colon cancer. Image credit: ©iStock.com, FalconScallagrim PDF version Share I mmunotherapies have dramatically improved outcomes for patients with cancer, but some patient populations, such as a large subset of individuals with colorectal cancer, respond poorly to these treatments. However, a potential way to boost these therapies lies with an unexpected source: the foodborne pathogen Listeria monocytogenes . In a new study in mice, researchers found that ingestion of attenuated L. monocytogenes as an oral cancer vaccine elicited a cytotoxic T cell response in the gut and transiently halted colorectal tumor growth. 1 Co-administration of immune checkpoint inhibitors sustained this effect, highlighting a potential new path to harnessing the immune system against these deadly cancers. An Oral Vaccine Route for a Foodborne Pathogen-Based Therapy Prior L. monocytogenes -based vaccines were delivered intravenously to help them bypass the body’s natural defenses, but this route can lead to sepsis on rare occasions since the bacteria get delivered directly into the bloodstream. 2 The oral vaccine route, on the other hand, impressed Laurence Wood , an immunologist at Texas Tech University who was not involved in the study and who had previously developed an intravenous L. monocytogenes -based vaccine. 3 “The natural route of infection for Listeria is foodborne, so it makes sense to leverage that aspect of it,” Wood said. “I think it’s promising that it looks like work is going in this way.” Continue reading below... Sign up for FREE Cancer updates: Latest science news stories Topic-tailored resources and events Customized newsletter content Subscribe Study coauthor Semir Beyaz , a cancer biologist at Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory, added, “We think that it’s safer than what’s currently being used in clinical trials for Listeria. ” Researchers develop cancer vaccines using L. monocytogenes because the bacteria contain the protein internalin A, which binds to human E-cadherin, a protein that is often upregulated in tumors. 4 This allows L. monocytogenes to invade the cancer cells, and the bacteria’s presence calls immune cells to previously poorly immunogenic tumors. To test an L. monocytogenes -based vaccine in mice, the researchers first mutated it so that it could interact with the mouse E-cadherin protein. They then inoculated a piece of bread with the unattenuated bacteria and fed it to mice. For comparison, the researchers also administered L. monocytogenes to the animals intravenously. Oral administration of L. monocytogenes induced T cells to take up residence in the intestinal mucosa significantly more than when the bacteria were delivered intravenously. Residency is an important characteristic for conferring rapid immune response in the organ. The population of resident T cells remained high over three months after infection, demonstrating that orally administered L. monocytogenes could indeed produce a robust immune response. To make the vaccine safe, the team deleted genes associated with L. monocytogenes pathogenicity. The number of attenuated bacteria in the mouse intestine was comparable to the bacteria’s unattenuated counterparts. However, attenuated L. monocytogenes was hardly detectable in other organs, such as the spleen and liver, demonstrating that the bacteria stayed local and within the target organ, which suggested a lower risk for sepsis. Like their unattenuated counterparts, attenuated L. monocytogenes also induced T cell residency in the intestinal mucosa. Altogether, these results suggest that the vaccine with attenuated bacteria is safe in mice. A Listeria -Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Combo Targets Colon Cancer Next, the researchers evaluated the oral vaccine’s impact on cancer. The team implanted a mouse colon cancer cell line into the colon’s lining 10 days after immunization with attenuated L. monocytogenes . Nearly all the vaccinated mice's tumors shrank within a week after they were immunized. This contrasted with their sham-immunized counterparts, whose tumors grew significantly in that period. The researchers also tested the vaccine’s therapeutic potential. To do this, they immunized the animals a week before transplanting tumor organoids into their colons. Similarly, this approach considerably halted tumor growth compared to the control groups, but the suppression didn’t last and hardly improved survival. The team hypothesized that the activated T cells might have activated immune checkpoints, which in turn, dampened the resulting immune response. So, starting five days after immunization, the researchers also treated the mice with immune checkpoint inhibitors every other day for two weeks. Compared with either the vaccine or inhibitor treatment alone, the combination therapy significantly suppressed mouse tumor growth for nearly 40 days. Continue reading below... He didn’t think it would be a good idea to have people eat Listeria -contaminated food even if the bacteria were attenuated. To him, the approach the researchers used “doesn’t seem like it’s easily translatable.” Wood added, “I wouldn’t give it in bread because then you’re getting it also in your mouth,” suggesting more traditional oral formulation such as capsules. But Beyaz and his team are optimistic. They hope that their work may lay the foundation for future clinical trials. “[This study] is a good proof of principle to show how you can use a Listeria vaccine to turn an incurable form of colon cancer in combination with immunotherapy,” said Beyaz. “That’s what I’m really excited about.” References Lei X, et al. May 12, 2026 | 7 min read Save for Later Companion diagnostics enable more precise trials, faster development cycles, and better health outcomes for some of the world’s sickest patients. Image credit: © iStock.com, Yuuji PDF version Register for free to listen to this article Listen with Speechify 0:00 7:00 Share T he path to bringing a new drug to market is increasingly complex and costly, with development costs now exceeding $2 billion and timelines approaching a decade. 1,2 The stakes have never been higher—demanding new models, new technologies, and new thinking to reduce risk and accelerate breakthroughs. Up to 90 percent of compounds entering clinical trials never reach the market, often due to unforeseen toxicity or lack of efficacy in heterogenous patient populations. This high failure rate has accelerated a shift toward more targeted development strategies. Companion diagnostics are central to this shift, enabling more precise trials, faster development cycles, and better health outcomes for some of the world’s sickest patients. Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the landscape—not only for therapeutics but also for precision diagnostics that guide patient selection and treatment decisions. Digital pathology and AI now sit at the heart of this transformation, offering new ways to extract quantitative biological signals, harmonize global lab variability, and support earlier, sharper decision‑making in clinical trials. 3 From Failure to Focus: Reducing Drug Development Risk with Computational Pathology Biology is heterogeneous, traditional pathology is variable, and global clinical trial operations introduce noise that can obscure early efficacy or safety signals. 4 Whole‑slide imaging (WSI) and computational pathology have the potential to directly address these challenges by scaling objective readouts from tissue and associated morphology with clinical outcomes. Continue reading below... Like this story? Sign up for FREE Cancer updates: Latest science news stories Topic-tailored resources and events Customized newsletter content Subscribe With over 15 years of experience in diagnostics and pathology, I have seen how “identical” hematoxylin & eosin (H&E) slides can vary across sites—introducing noise, repeat reviews, and delayed decisions. This becomes particularly challenging when variability forces the tissue journey to restart, or worse, necessitates repeat tissue collection from patients, many of whom are critically ill—consuming precious, often irreplaceable patient samples and driving additional trial costs. AI‑enabled tissue quantification has the potential to address these challenges by reducing subjectivity, delivering more reproducible endpoints, and generating cleaner data earlier in drug development. AI can also serve as a second set of eyes during review, helping ensure critical features are not missed and increasing confidence in study outcomes. From Slides to Quantitative Biomarkers Modern AI models are capable of identifying subtle morphologic patterns that correlate with prognosis, molecular status, and treatment response. For example, multiple‑instance learning (MIL)-based approaches have matured to clinical‑grade performance for predicting histology-derived endpoints, providing objective, reproducible metrics appropriate for global deployment and regulatory evaluation. 5 These biomarkers further reduce biological uncertainty by enabling earlier biological signal detection and quantitative features that can be deployed consistently across global trials. This shift allows development teams to detect trends long before traditional clinical endpoints mature. 6 Strengthening Oncology Trial Decisions Through Early AI‑Enabled Signal Detection AI‑enabled biomarkers support early patient stratification, reduce biological and operational noise, and enable more accurate response prediction across oncology trials . Increasingly, studies demonstrate that morphology‑derived signatures extracted from routine histology can predict outcomes and drug response earlier—and often more reproducibly—than traditional clinical readouts. 6 This is particularly relevant in immuno‑oncology, where response to therapy is shaped by both tumor-intrinsic features and the tumor microenvironment. While established biomarkers such as PD‑L1 immunohistochemistry have been central to patient selection, they only capture part of this biological complexity. In this context, weakly supervised AI models applied to standard H&E sections can infer tumor microenvironment characteristics and immunotherapy response at scale, complementing PD-L1 based strategies and enabling earlier enrichment and informed decisions for treatment optimization. 3,6 Bridging the R&D–to–Real‑World Gap in CDx Development Companion diagnostics (CDx) failures often occur not during discovery, but at deployment—when real‑world laboratory variability undermines analytical performance. Multi‑center datasets consistently demonstrate significant inter-laboratory variation in staining and scanning, driving domain shift and degrading model performance unless proactively managed. 7 Recent studies underscore how stain‑normalization techniques are evolving to address this challenge. Methods such as Macenko, Reinhard, and Vahadane continue to serve as strong and reliable baselines, sustaining their role as workhorses in digital pathology workflows. In parallel, generative adversarial network‑based and hybrid approaches are demonstrating clear advantages in cross‑site robustness, enabling models to generalize more effectively across heterogeneous scanners and staining protocols. Most notably, techniques, such as stain‑aware normalization and Beer–Lambert-based models, offer substantial reductions in performance loss under shifting staining conditions, representing a meaningful advance toward more resilient and deployment‑ready image analysis pipelines. These capabilities are critical for achieving analytically valid CDx deployment across global laboratory networks. 8 Infrastructure Readiness: Cloud‑Native, Compliant, and Audit‑Ready Digital pathology infrastructure continues to mature globally, with cloud‑native, compliant, and fully auditable platforms emerging as the foundation for scalable deployment. The FDA clearance of WSI for primary diagnosis has further facilitated adoption, enabling clinical‑grade digital pathology infrastructure to operate reliably and securely across institutions. Importantly, the infrastructure readiness in AI-enabled pathology extends beyond software and cloud architecture to the full end-to-end system, from tissue handling to computational analysis. At present, glass slides remain the biological ground truth, supporting regulatory review, retrospective analysis, and future biomarker discovery. Not all whole-slide scanners are equivalent in optical quality, color fidelity, throughput, or reproducibility. These differences can have a significant impact on downstream algorithm performance if not carefully controlled. As AI-derived endpoints move into registrational trials and companion diagnostic deployment, the selection of clinically validated, high-performance scanning platforms become a critical component of infrastructure readiness. In parallel, regulatory expectations for AI in healthcare are becoming increasingly well defined, with greater emphasis on adherence to Good Machine Learning Practice (GMLP), transparency in AI‑generated outputs, and robust oversight across the total product lifecycle—including proactive post‑market monitoring.  For AI-enabled assays, this includes controls such as cell line and reference material controls, locked models, cross-lab performance monitoring, and auditable data lineage. Cloud‑native pipelines, designed to meet HIPAA/GDPR requirements, can now offer essential capabilities such as comprehensive audit trails, encryption, role‑based access control, and data lineage. Together, these developments support deployment-ready, regulator-aligned digital pathology workflows for next-generation companion diagnostics and clinical decision support. Regional CDx Regulatory Landscape In the US, the FDA provides relatively clear CDx co‑development pathways , supported by oncology‑focused pilot programs that encourage early alignment between therapeutic and diagnostic development. In Europe, the In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation (IVDR) elevates CDx to Class C, requiring Notified Body review and consultation with the European Medicines Agency . While this shift strengthens regulatory rigor and oversight, it also introduces increased workload, operational complexity, and longer development timelines. Comparative analyses show widening differences between FDA and IVDR requirements—underscoring the importance of coordinated, early regulatory planning. Without proactive alignment, these regional differences can introduce delays, rework, and downstream risk to global CDx deployment. AI Augmenting Pathologists Workflows AI has the potential to improve diagnostic accuracy, standardization, and efficiency in pathology. However, contextual interpretation, clinical judgement, and patient‑impacting decisions remain firmly within the expertise of the pathologist. Reviews continue to emphasize that safe and effective use of AI requires clinician‑in‑the‑loop workflows, where human oversight is integral to decision‑making. 9,10 As a cyto- and histopathologist, I have spent countless hours performing manual, time‑intensive tasks such as accurately counting inflammatory cells to diagnose acute bladder inflammation or enumerating mitotic figures to determine breast cancer grade, decisions that directly influence patient treatment. AI has the potential to relieve pathologists of these repetitive, low-value tasks, allowing us to focus on integrative reasoning, clinical context, and complex diagnostic synthesis—capabilities that algorithms cannot replicate. The Future: Multimodal, Generalizable, and Equitable Next‑generation multimodal foundation models integrate histology with clinical reports, genomics, and proteomics to improve disease classification, survival prediction, and biological interpretability across cancer types. These models move beyond single‑modality analysis, enabling richer context and more biologically meaningful insights. 8 When rigorously validated across sites and paired with stain‑robust deployment‑ready pipelines, these systems have the potential to expand access to precision diagnostics globally, including in low‑resource settings where specialist expertise and advanced infrastructure may be limited. 3,11 Importantly, AI is not a substitute for skilled laboratory staff and researchers; rather it serves as a powerful second set of eyes—enhancing precision, increasing agility, and elevating the quality of scientific work with deeper insights. Collaboration Delivers Greater Value In an environment where accelerating time‑to‑market is increasingly critical, building diagnostics capabilities from scratch can introduce unnecessary cost, delay, and execution risk. Strategic collaboration offers a more efficient path forward, allowing innovation to scale without sacrificing rigor or speed. Beyond operational efficiency, collaboration also enables a departure from traditional CDx partnership models that often constrain speed and flexibility. Emerging platform-based, data-centric approaches allow therapeutic and diagnostic development to progress in parallel, reducing hand-offs, compressing timelines, and enabling faster launches. Importantly, these models support earlier alignment on evidence generation, regulatory strategy, and global deployment—reducing late-stage friction that has historically delayed market entry. Partnerships are helping build comprehensive antibody libraries, powered by sophisticated AI analysis. Instead of starting anew, pharmaceutical companies can leverage robust, pre‑validated datasets to establish proof‑of‑concept more rapidly and with greater confidence. For emerging biomarkers, the platform’s ability to generate custom antibodies on demand adds critical flexibility and speed. Looking Ahead: A New Model for Evidence Generation As personalized medicine becomes the standard of care, the pressure on pharmaceutical companies to develop robust companion diagnostics has never been greater—elevating risk mitigation capabilities from operational considerations to sources of competitive advantage. AI is emerging as the new scientific lens for drug development and CDx. By reducing biological uncertainty, harmonizing variability across global laboratory networks, and supporting earlier, more confident decision‑making, AI is accelerating the path from discovery to meaningful patient impact. Critically, the next evolution of evidence generation will integrate real-world evidence (RWE) with clinical trial data. When combined with AI-enabled diagnostics, RWE enables ongoing validation of biomarker performance across more diverse patient populations, strengthening confidence in clinical utility beyond controlled trials. This approach allows best practices to be scaled more rapidly, accelerating the translation of approved innovations into meaningful patient impact. As cloud‑based pathology infrastructure continues to mature and regulatory frameworks for AI diagnostics evolve, these technologies will increasingly define how evidence is generated, validated, and translated into the next generation of precision therapeutics. News Bread-Based Bacterial Vaccine Boosted Colon Cancer Therapy in Mice When combined with immune checkpoint inhibitors, bread coated in attenuated Listeria stimulated a gut immune response and suppressed colorectal tumor growth in mice. Written by Andrea Lius, PhD Andrea Lius, PhD Andrea Lius is a freelance science writer. She is working on her PhD in pharmacology at the University of Washington in Seattle. View Full Profile Learn about our Editorial Policies . Apr 20, 2026 | 3 min read Save for Later An oral cancer vaccine containing non-pathogenic Listeria paired with immune checkpoint inhibitors could lead to a new way to treat colon cancer. Image credit: ©iStock.com, FalconScallagrim PDF version Share I mmunotherapies have dramatically improved outcomes for patients with cancer, but some patient populations, such as a large subset of individuals with colorectal cancer, respond poorly to these treatments. However, a potential way to boost these therapies lies with an unexpected source: the foodborne pathogen Listeria monocytogenes . In a new study in mice, researchers found that ingestion of attenuated L. monocytogenes as an oral cancer vaccine elicited a cytotoxic T cell response in the gut and transiently halted colorectal tumor growth. 1 Co-administration of immune checkpoint inhibitors sustained this effect, highlighting a potential new path to harnessing the immune system against these deadly cancers. An Oral Vaccine Route for a Foodborne Pathogen-Based Therapy Prior L. monocytogenes -based vaccines were delivered intravenously to help them bypass the body’s natural defenses, but this route can lead to sepsis on rare occasions since the bacteria get delivered directly into the bloodstream. 2 The oral vaccine route, on the other hand, impressed Laurence Wood , an immunologist at Texas Tech University who was not involved in the study and who had previously developed an intravenous L. monocytogenes -based vaccine. 3 “The natural route of infection for Listeria is foodborne, so it makes sense to leverage that aspect of it,” Wood said. “I think it’s promising that it looks like work is going in this way.” Continue reading below... Like this story? Sign up for FREE Cancer updates: Latest science news stories Topic-tailored resources and events Customized newsletter content Subscribe Study coauthor Semir Beyaz , a cancer biologist at Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory, added, “We think that it’s safer than what’s currently being used in clinical trials for Listeria. ” Researchers develop cancer vaccines using L. monocytogenes because the bacteria contain the protein internalin A, which binds to human E-cadherin, a protein that is often upregulated in tumors. 4 This allows L. monocytogenes to invade the cancer cells, and the bacteria’s presence calls immune cells to previously poorly immunogenic tumors. To test an L. monocytogenes -based vaccine in mice, the researchers first mutated it so that it could interact with the mouse E-cadherin protein. They then inoculated a piece of bread with the unattenuated bacteria and fed it to mice. For comparison, the researchers also administered L. monocytogenes to the animals intravenously. Oral administration of L. monocytogenes induced T cells to take up residence in the intestinal mucosa significantly more than when the bacteria were delivered intravenously. Residency is an important characteristic for conferring rapid immune response in the organ. The population of resident T cells remained high over three months after infection, demonstrating that orally administered L. monocytogenes could indeed produce a robust immune response. To make the vaccine safe, the team deleted genes associated with L. monocytogenes pathogenicity. The number of attenuated bacteria in the mouse intestine was comparable to the bacteria’s unattenuated counterparts. However, attenuated L. monocytogenes was hardly detectable in other organs, such as the spleen and liver, demonstrating that the bacteria stayed local and within the target organ, which suggested a lower risk for sepsis. Like their unattenuated counterparts, attenuated L. monocytogenes also induced T cell residency in the intestinal mucosa. Altogether, these results suggest that the vaccine with attenuated bacteria is safe in mice. A Listeria -Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Combo Targets Colon Cancer Next, the researchers evaluated the oral vaccine’s impact on cancer. The team implanted a mouse colon cancer cell line into the colon’s lining 10 days after immunization with attenuated L. monocytogenes . Nearly all the vaccinated mice's tumors shrank within a week after they were immunized. This contrasted with their sham-immunized counterparts, whose tumors grew significantly in that period. The researchers also tested the vaccine’s therapeutic potential. To do this, they immunized the animals a week before transplanting tumor organoids into their colons. Similarly, this approach considerably halted tumor growth compared to the control groups, but the suppression didn’t last and hardly improved survival. The team hypothesized that the activated T cells might have activated immune checkpoints, which in turn, dampened the resulting immune response. So, starting five days after immunization, the researchers also treated the mice with immune checkpoint inhibitors every other day for two weeks. Compared with either the vaccine or inhibitor treatment alone, the combination therapy significantly suppressed mouse tumor growth for nearly 40 days. Continue reading below... He didn’t think it would be a good idea to have people eat Listeria -contaminated food even if the bacteria were attenuated. To him, the approach the researchers used “doesn’t seem like it’s easily translatable.” Wood added, “I wouldn’t give it in bread because then you’re getting it also in your mouth,” suggesting more traditional oral formulation such as capsules. But Beyaz and his team are optimistic. They hope that their work may lay the foundation for future clinical trials. “[This study] is a good proof of principle to show how you can use a Listeria vaccine to turn an incurable form of colon cancer in combination with immunotherapy,” said Beyaz. “That’s what I’m really excited about.” References Lei X, et al. The number of attenuated bacteria in the mouse intestine was comparable to the bacteria’s unattenuated counterparts. However, attenuated L. monocytogenes was hardly detectable in other organs, such as the spleen and liver, demonstrating that the bacteria stayed local and within the target organ, which suggested a lower risk for sepsis. Like their unattenuated counterparts, attenuated L. monocytogenes also induced T cell residency in the intestinal mucosa. Altogether, these results suggest that the vaccine with attenuated bacteria is safe in mice. A Listeria -Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Combo Targets Colon Cancer Next, the researchers evaluated the oral vaccine’s impact on cancer. The team implanted a mouse colon cancer cell line into the colon’s lining 10 days after immunization with attenuated L. monocytogenes . Nearly all the vaccinated mice's tumors shrank within a week after they were immunized. This contrasted with their sham-immunized counterparts, whose tumors grew significantly in that period. The researchers also tested the vaccine’s therapeutic potential. To do this, they immunized the animals a week before transplanting tumor organoids into their colons. Similarly, this approach considerably halted tumor growth compared to the control groups, but the suppression didn’t last and hardly improved survival. The team hypothesized that the activated T cells might have activated immune checkpoints, which in turn, dampened the resulting immune response. So, starting five days after immunization, the researchers also treated the mice with immune checkpoint inhibitors every other day for two weeks. Compared with either the vaccine or inhibitor treatment alone, the combination therapy significantly suppressed mouse tumor growth for nearly 40 days. Continue reading below... I mmunotherapies have dramatically improved outcomes for patients with cancer, but some patient populations, such as a large subset of individuals with colorectal cancer, respond poorly to these treatments. However, a potential way to boost these therapies lies with an unexpected source: the foodborne pathogen Listeria monocytogenes .
I
mmunotherapies
Listeria monocytogenes
In a new study in mice, researchers found that ingestion of attenuated L. monocytogenes as an oral cancer vaccine elicited a cytotoxic T cell response in the gut and transiently halted colorectal tumor growth. 1 Co-administration of immune checkpoint inhibitors sustained this effect, highlighting a potential new path to harnessing the immune system against these deadly cancers.
L. monocytogenes
cancer vaccine
1
An Oral Vaccine Route for a Foodborne Pathogen-Based Therapy
Prior L. monocytogenes -based vaccines were delivered intravenously to help them bypass the body’s natural defenses, but this route can lead to sepsis on rare occasions since the bacteria get delivered directly into the bloodstream. 2 The oral vaccine route, on the other hand, impressed Laurence Wood , an immunologist at Texas Tech University who was not involved in the study and who had previously developed an intravenous L. monocytogenes -based vaccine. 3
2
oral vaccine
Laurence Wood
“The natural route of infection for Listeria is foodborne, so it makes sense to leverage that aspect of it,” Wood said. “I think it’s promising that it looks like work is going in this way.”
Study coauthor Semir Beyaz , a cancer biologist at Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory, added, “We think that it’s safer than what’s currently being used in clinical trials for Listeria. ”
Semir Beyaz
Listeria.
Researchers develop cancer vaccines using L. monocytogenes because the bacteria contain the protein internalin A, which binds to human E-cadherin, a protein that is often upregulated in tumors. 4 This allows L. monocytogenes to invade the cancer cells, and the bacteria’s presence calls immune cells to previously poorly immunogenic tumors.
To test an L. monocytogenes -based vaccine in mice, the researchers first mutated it so that it could interact with the mouse E-cadherin protein. They then inoculated a piece of bread with the unattenuated bacteria and fed it to mice. For comparison, the researchers also administered L. monocytogenes to the animals intravenously.
Oral administration of L. monocytogenes induced T cells to take up residence in the intestinal mucosa significantly more than when the bacteria were delivered intravenously. Residency is an important characteristic for conferring rapid immune response in the organ. articles.title: Nuclera launches antibody triage service to advance AI-driven antibody discovery
articles.text:
Skip to main content Product Nuclera launches antibody triage service to advance AI-driven antibody discovery Rapid binder triage, of AI-driven candidate sets, enables early elimination of non-binders ahead of costly downstream workflows Written by Nuclera Nuclera Nuclera’s mission is to better human health by enabling scientists to easily access the proteins they need for drug discovery research. The Company’s eProtein Discovery™ benchtop System accelerates protein expression and purification optimization in research labs. View Full Profile Learn about our Editorial Policies . May 11, 2026 | 2 min read Save for Later PDF version Register for free to listen to this article Listen with Speechify 0:00 2:00 Share Nuclera, the biotechnology company enabling rapid access to high-quality proteins, today announced the launch of its antibody screening service to streamline the transition from antibody hit generation to lead selection. The service will support researchers seeking to identify the most promising antibody candidates to progress to costly mammalian expression and functional testing, addressing a key bottleneck in AI-driven antibody discovery. The launch follows the Company’s Series C extension, enabling the integration of antibody expression and binding validation to support antibody discovery workflows. Nuclera’s antibody service delivers a rapid upstream triage workflow that identifies viable binders early on in the process between in silico hit generation and mammalian scale-up. By utilizing 96-plex binary cell-free expression and binding assays, the service screens full length antibody libraries in parallel, rapidly narrowing large candidate sets to a focused subset of confirmed binders. Surface Plasmon Resonance is then performed on prioritized hits for binding kinetics. Despite advances in bioinformatics and in silico antibody design, a major bottleneck remains in experimentally validating large numbers of candidates. Traditional antibody secondary screening methods are often slow and fragmented, which typically result in large amounts of resources being spent on non-binders through costly processes. As AI-driven approaches generate increasingly large antibody libraries, the need for rapid, cost-effective triage solutions has become more critical. Nuclera’s antibody service addresses this gap by converting large AI-generated libraries into experimental binding data and enabling early elimination of non-binders, reserving expensive downstream biology for candidates proven to bind and accelerating progression to validated leads. Dr Michael Chen, CEO and co-founder, Nuclera, said: “Antibodies are one of the most important classes of therapeutic molecules, yet antibody discovery remains inefficient, with many initially promising candidates failing during downstream validation. A key bottleneck is the cost of recombinant antibody expression and binding validation, which limits the generation of high-quality data, and is holding back the full potential of AI/ML discovery. The launch of our antibody service addresses this challenge by enabling rapid triage of large candidate sets and delivering decision-grade binding data early in the discovery process at a competitive cost. By helping teams focus on the most promising candidates before scale-up, we are taking an important step toward enabling more effective use of AI in antibody discovery.” Add The Scientist as a preferred Google source to see more of our trusted coverage. Interview Using Domesticated Microbes to Fight Infection Lena Pernas discusses how mitochondria act as cellular defenders by competing with parasites like Toxoplasma gondii for vital nutrients. Written by Hannah Pletcher Hannah Pletcher Hannah Pletcher is working towards a PhD in biochemistry at Washington University in St. Louis, studying fundamental mitochondrial metabolism and metabolic protein regulation. View Full Profile Learn about our Editorial Policies . Mar 25, 2026 | 3 min read Save for Later New insights into parasitic infection show how mitochondria can limit pathogen growth by competing for essential nutrients within host cells. Image credit: © iStock.com, Dr_Microbe PDF version Share L ena Pernas had an early fascination with infectious disease that has expanded to include the role of mitochondria—which she dubs domesticated microbes—as cellular defenders against infection. After first establishing a laboratory at the Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing, she recently returned to her undergraduate institution, the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), to research the metabolism of infection using Toxoplasma gondii as a model system. How did you become interested in infectious diseases? My father was always trying to get my siblings and me curious about something, so he brought home different books and games that would pique our interest. The Oregon Trail had a fun cousin game called The Amazon Trail . The goal was to go down the Amazon River, where different things could happen to each player. I was fascinated that you could get malaria, and then you had to find the Cinchona tree to cure yourself. I also loved the glossary that contained all the infectious diseases that one could contract in the Amazon. That is what started my obsession with parasites. From an early fascination with infectious diseases to leading her own lab at UCLA, Lena Pernas studies how mitochondria function as cellular defenders against parasitic infection. Kristen Neumann/AP Images for HHMI Was that the moment you decided to pursue a career in research? I knew I loved science and disease, so I wanted to be a doctor. As a kid, I thought that the only way to discover science was through medicine. At UCLA, I decided to study microbiology. Then, a friend of my sister's was in an incredible program called Maximizing Access to Research Careers (MARC). It was an NIH-funded, two-year fellowship for undergraduates that paid awardees to do research. When I learned about scientific research through this program, I thought, this is what I've been looking for. I applied, was accepted, and started working in Kent Hill 's laboratory studying trypanosomes, a parasite that causes sleeping sickness. I do not think there was ever another path for me after I learned about research. Continue reading below... Like this story? Sign up for FREE Microbiology updates: Latest science news stories Topic-tailored resources and events Customized newsletter content Subscribe What has it been like returning to UCLA as an assistant professor? It has been amazing. I was initially concerned that I would feel like a child because many of the folks in this department are people that I took classes with as an undergraduate. I felt like there would always be this “I'm still a pupil” mentality, but they have never treated me as such. I have a wonderful community of amazing colleagues that are welcoming, supportive, and collaborative. Members of the Pernas lab at UCLA study how host metabolism changes to defend against parasites such as Toxoplasma gondii . Temitope Ademolue, PhD What sparked your interest in the role of mitochondria during infection? A lot of my current research started in graduate school with my PhD advisor, John Boothroyd . He showed me electron micrographs of monocytes that had been isolated from mice infected with Toxoplasma gondii . For me, one of the most striking consequences of infection was that the mitochondria surrounded the vacuole that the parasite resided in. I thought this was fascinating and wondered why the mitochondria were doing that. So, I explored the molecular mechanism that binds the parasite vacuole to the mitochondria. 1 However, the mitochondria that were attached to a Toxoplasma -containing vacuole were elongated and had a different shape than the mitochondria in uninfected cells. The traditional perspective from a microbiologist was that the parasite is exploiting the mitochondria, but towards the end of my PhD program, I began to think that maybe the host is trying to do something to the parasites using mitochondria. In my postdoctoral fellowship in Luca Scorrano 's laboratory, I found that the changes in mitochondrial shape seem to correlate with changes in their metabolism. 2 Healthy, elongated mitochondria take up fatty acids, limiting the fatty acids available to the parasites. This was the first hint that maybe there is nutrient competition between the invading parasite and the mitochondria. What are you studying now? The concept of nutrient competition between mitochondria and parasites was a foundation for other questions, including work started by an incredible postdoctoral fellow in my laboratory, Tânia Medeiros . Thinking about mitochondria as domesticated microbes, they need a lot of resources from the host cell. What if parasites also need those resources? She was able to discover a response where host cells sense a pathogen and use the integrated stress response pathway to sequester folate in the mitochondria, depriving Toxoplasma gondii of this vitamin, which it needs for its own replication. 3 This was another exciting example of how mitochondria and invading pathogens can compete for nutrients. This was also a fun example of how one can use infection as a lens to study mitochondrial metabolism in infection-independent scenarios. The interview has been condensed and edited for clarity. References Pernas L, et al. Toxoplasma effector MAF1 mediates recruitment of host mitochondria and impacts the host response . PloS Biol. 2014;12(4):e1001845. Pernas L, et al. Mitochondria protect against an intracellular pathogen by restricting access to folate . Science. 2025;389(6761):eadr6326. May 11, 2026 | 2 min read Save for Later PDF version Register for free to listen to this article Listen with Speechify 0:00 2:00 Share Nuclera, the biotechnology company enabling rapid access to high-quality proteins, today announced the launch of its antibody screening service to streamline the transition from antibody hit generation to lead selection. The service will support researchers seeking to identify the most promising antibody candidates to progress to costly mammalian expression and functional testing, addressing a key bottleneck in AI-driven antibody discovery. The launch follows the Company’s Series C extension, enabling the integration of antibody expression and binding validation to support antibody discovery workflows. Nuclera’s antibody service delivers a rapid upstream triage workflow that identifies viable binders early on in the process between in silico hit generation and mammalian scale-up. By utilizing 96-plex binary cell-free expression and binding assays, the service screens full length antibody libraries in parallel, rapidly narrowing large candidate sets to a focused subset of confirmed binders. Surface Plasmon Resonance is then performed on prioritized hits for binding kinetics. Despite advances in bioinformatics and in silico antibody design, a major bottleneck remains in experimentally validating large numbers of candidates. Nuclera’s antibody service addresses this gap by converting large AI-generated libraries into experimental binding data and enabling early elimination of non-binders, reserving expensive downstream biology for candidates proven to bind and accelerating progression to validated leads. Dr Michael Chen, CEO and co-founder, Nuclera, said: “Antibodies are one of the most important classes of therapeutic molecules, yet antibody discovery remains inefficient, with many initially promising candidates failing during downstream validation. A key bottleneck is the cost of recombinant antibody expression and binding validation, which limits the generation of high-quality data, and is holding back the full potential of AI/ML discovery. The launch of our antibody service addresses this challenge by enabling rapid triage of large candidate sets and delivering decision-grade binding data early in the discovery process at a competitive cost. By helping teams focus on the most promising candidates before scale-up, we are taking an important step toward enabling more effective use of AI in antibody discovery.” Add The Scientist as a preferred Google source to see more of our trusted coverage. Image credit: © iStock.com, Dr_Microbe PDF version Share L ena Pernas had an early fascination with infectious disease that has expanded to include the role of mitochondria—which she dubs domesticated microbes—as cellular defenders against infection. After first establishing a laboratory at the Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing, she recently returned to her undergraduate institution, the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), to research the metabolism of infection using Toxoplasma gondii as a model system. How did you become interested in infectious diseases? My father was always trying to get my siblings and me curious about something, so he brought home different books and games that would pique our interest. The Oregon Trail had a fun cousin game called The Amazon Trail . The goal was to go down the Amazon River, where different things could happen to each player. I was fascinated that you could get malaria, and then you had to find the Cinchona tree to cure yourself. I also loved the glossary that contained all the infectious diseases that one could contract in the Amazon. That is what started my obsession with parasites. From an early fascination with infectious diseases to leading her own lab at UCLA, Lena Pernas studies how mitochondria function as cellular defenders against parasitic infection. Kristen Neumann/AP Images for HHMI Was that the moment you decided to pursue a career in research? I knew I loved science and disease, so I wanted to be a doctor. As a kid, I thought that the only way to discover science was through medicine. At UCLA, I decided to study microbiology. Then, a friend of my sister's was in an incredible program called Maximizing Access to Research Careers (MARC). It was an NIH-funded, two-year fellowship for undergraduates that paid awardees to do research. When I learned about scientific research through this program, I thought, this is what I've been looking for. I applied, was accepted, and started working in Kent Hill 's laboratory studying trypanosomes, a parasite that causes sleeping sickness. I do not think there was ever another path for me after I learned about research. Continue reading below... Like this story? It has been amazing. I was initially concerned that I would feel like a child because many of the folks in this department are people that I took classes with as an undergraduate. I felt like there would always be this “I'm still a pupil” mentality, but they have never treated me as such. I have a wonderful community of amazing colleagues that are welcoming, supportive, and collaborative. Members of the Pernas lab at UCLA study how host metabolism changes to defend against parasites such as Toxoplasma gondii . Temitope Ademolue, PhD What sparked your interest in the role of mitochondria during infection? A lot of my current research started in graduate school with my PhD advisor, John Boothroyd . He showed me electron micrographs of monocytes that had been isolated from mice infected with Toxoplasma gondii . For me, one of the most striking consequences of infection was that the mitochondria surrounded the vacuole that the parasite resided in. I thought this was fascinating and wondered why the mitochondria were doing that. So, I explored the molecular mechanism that binds the parasite vacuole to the mitochondria. 1 However, the mitochondria that were attached to a Toxoplasma -containing vacuole were elongated and had a different shape than the mitochondria in uninfected cells. The traditional perspective from a microbiologist was that the parasite is exploiting the mitochondria, but towards the end of my PhD program, I began to think that maybe the host is trying to do something to the parasites using mitochondria. In my postdoctoral fellowship in Luca Scorrano 's laboratory, I found that the changes in mitochondrial shape seem to correlate with changes in their metabolism. 2 Healthy, elongated mitochondria take up fatty acids, limiting the fatty acids available to the parasites. This was the first hint that maybe there is nutrient competition between the invading parasite and the mitochondria. What are you studying now? The concept of nutrient competition between mitochondria and parasites was a foundation for other questions, including work started by an incredible postdoctoral fellow in my laboratory, Tânia Medeiros . Thinking about mitochondria as domesticated microbes, they need a lot of resources from the host cell. What if parasites also need those resources? She was able to discover a response where host cells sense a pathogen and use the integrated stress response pathway to sequester folate in the mitochondria, depriving Toxoplasma gondii of this vitamin, which it needs for its own replication. 3 This was another exciting example of how mitochondria and invading pathogens can compete for nutrients. This was also a fun example of how one can use infection as a lens to study mitochondrial metabolism in infection-independent scenarios. The interview has been condensed and edited for clarity. New insights into parasitic infection show how mitochondria can limit pathogen growth by competing for essential nutrients within host cells. Image credit: © iStock.com, Dr_Microbe PDF version Share L ena Pernas had an early fascination with infectious disease that has expanded to include the role of mitochondria—which she dubs domesticated microbes—as cellular defenders against infection. After first establishing a laboratory at the Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing, she recently returned to her undergraduate institution, the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), to research the metabolism of infection using Toxoplasma gondii as a model system. How did you become interested in infectious diseases? My father was always trying to get my siblings and me curious about something, so he brought home different books and games that would pique our interest. The Oregon Trail had a fun cousin game called The Amazon Trail . The goal was to go down the Amazon River, where different things could happen to each player. I was fascinated that you could get malaria, and then you had to find the Cinchona tree to cure yourself. I also loved the glossary that contained all the infectious diseases that one could contract in the Amazon. That is what started my obsession with parasites. From an early fascination with infectious diseases to leading her own lab at UCLA, Lena Pernas studies how mitochondria function as cellular defenders against parasitic infection. Kristen Neumann/AP Images for HHMI Was that the moment you decided to pursue a career in research? I knew I loved science and disease, so I wanted to be a doctor. As a kid, I thought that the only way to discover science was through medicine. At UCLA, I decided to study microbiology. Then, a friend of my sister's was in an incredible program called Maximizing Access to Research Careers (MARC). It was an NIH-funded, two-year fellowship for undergraduates that paid awardees to do research. When I learned about scientific research through this program, I thought, this is what I've been looking for. I applied, was accepted, and started working in Kent Hill 's laboratory studying trypanosomes, a parasite that causes sleeping sickness. I do not think there was ever another path for me after I learned about research. Continue reading below... Like this story? It has been amazing. I was initially concerned that I would feel like a child because many of the folks in this department are people that I took classes with as an undergraduate. I felt like there would always be this “I'm still a pupil” mentality, but they have never treated me as such. I have a wonderful community of amazing colleagues that are welcoming, supportive, and collaborative. Members of the Pernas lab at UCLA study how host metabolism changes to defend against parasites such as Toxoplasma gondii . Temitope Ademolue, PhD What sparked your interest in the role of mitochondria during infection? A lot of my current research started in graduate school with my PhD advisor, John Boothroyd . He showed me electron micrographs of monocytes that had been isolated from mice infected with Toxoplasma gondii . For me, one of the most striking consequences of infection was that the mitochondria surrounded the vacuole that the parasite resided in. I thought this was fascinating and wondered why the mitochondria were doing that. So, I explored the molecular mechanism that binds the parasite vacuole to the mitochondria. 1 However, the mitochondria that were attached to a Toxoplasma -containing vacuole were elongated and had a different shape than the mitochondria in uninfected cells. The traditional perspective from a microbiologist was that the parasite is exploiting the mitochondria, but towards the end of my PhD program, I began to think that maybe the host is trying to do something to the parasites using mitochondria. In my postdoctoral fellowship in Luca Scorrano 's laboratory, I found that the changes in mitochondrial shape seem to correlate with changes in their metabolism. 2 Healthy, elongated mitochondria take up fatty acids, limiting the fatty acids available to the parasites. This was the first hint that maybe there is nutrient competition between the invading parasite and the mitochondria. What are you studying now? The concept of nutrient competition between mitochondria and parasites was a foundation for other questions, including work started by an incredible postdoctoral fellow in my laboratory, Tânia Medeiros . Thinking about mitochondria as domesticated microbes, they need a lot of resources from the host cell. What if parasites also need those resources? She was able to discover a response where host cells sense a pathogen and use the integrated stress response pathway to sequester folate in the mitochondria, depriving Toxoplasma gondii of this vitamin, which it needs for its own replication. 3 This was another exciting example of how mitochondria and invading pathogens can compete for nutrients. This was also a fun example of how one can use infection as a lens to study mitochondrial metabolism in infection-independent scenarios. The interview has been condensed and edited for clarity. References Pernas L, et al. Toxoplasma effector MAF1 mediates recruitment of host mitochondria and impacts the host response . PloS Biol. 2014;12(4):e1001845. Pernas L, et al. Mitochondria restrict growth of the intracellular parasite Toxoplasma gondii by limiting its uptake of fatty acids . Cell Metab. 2018;27(4):886-897. Medeiros TC, et al. Mitochondria protect against an intracellular pathogen by restricting access to folate . Science. 2025;389(6761):eadr6326. articles.title: Chicken Eggs Become Bioreactors to Brew Low-Cost Medicines
articles.text:
Skip to main content Interview Chicken Eggs Become Bioreactors to Brew Low-Cost Medicines Neion Bio uses genetically engineered chickens to produce therapeutic proteins in eggs, aiming for a drastic reduction in the cost of biologics manufacturing. Written by Meenakshi Prabhune, PhD Meenakshi Prabhune, PhD Go to The Scientist's LinkedIn Page Meenakshi is the Editor-in-Chief at The Scientist . Her diverse science communication experience includes journalism, podcasting, and content strategy. Meenakshi earned her PhD in biophysics from the University of Goettingen, Germany. View Full Profile Learn about our Editorial Policies . May 11, 2026 | 4 min read Save for Later The Neion Bio team engineers chicken to express therapeutic human proteins within the egg white. Image credit: Marco Figueroa PDF version Register for free to listen to this article Listen with Speechify 0:00 4:00 Share S amuel Levin, cofounder and chief technical officer of Neion Bio, opened his talk at Synbiobeta 2026 with the inefficiencies of current biomanufacturing processes. Most biological medicines are predominantly manufactured in massive bioreactors, primarily utilizing Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells. However, Levin pointed out that this cell type became an industry standard not because of its efficiency or merits, but because it was one of the few cell types scientists could engineer a few decades ago. Yet, the industry pours a staggering amount of money into keeping the system functional. Facilities required to house these cellular bioreactors often cost hundreds of millions or even billions of dollars, and the resulting biological products can cost up to thousands of dollars per gram to produce. Neion Bio, which emerged from stealth in 2026, proposes a radical departure from this hardware-heavy history. Founded by evolutionary biologist Levin and aerospace engineer Dimi Kellari , the company seeks to replace nearly every component of the modern bioprocessing facility with nature’s most prolific protein factory: the chicken egg. Neion Bio’s team genetically engineers chickens so they lay eggs with the desired proteins, and the team extracts these downstream. According to Levin, a single chicken farm, small enough to fit within a standard laboratory could theoretically produce the global supply of a blockbuster biologic like Humira. Samuel Levin (left), chief technology officer, and Dimi Killari (right), chief executive officer, co-founded Neion Bio to simplify biomanufacturing. Marco Figueroa “We essentially farm medicines,” Levin said of the company’s autonomous, self-replicating, and scalable bioreactor system. Continue reading below... Like this story? Sign up for FREE Cell Biology updates: Latest science news stories Topic-tailored resources and events Customized newsletter content Subscribe In an interview after their talk, the leadership team at Neion Bio—Levin and Kellari, the company’s cofounder and chief executive officer—discussed the technological breakthroughs and economic imperatives driving their mission to democratize access to life-changing medicines. The Genesis of the Avian Bioreactor How did you get the idea of using chicken eggs as bioreactors? Levin: Like most things in science, we're building on decades of research by other people. My cofounder Dimi and I were fixated on this problem, which is that while AI dramatically reduces the time and cost to discover and design new proteins, the way we actually make these proteins in the real world hasn't changed in 15 years and remains very inefficient. So, we spent a ton of time questioning why we make proteins in giant steel tanks and CHO cells. How else could we do this? What would the ideal bioprocess look like? In the middle of this deep problem searching, we came across a paper from 20 years ago, where a team worked on genetically engineering chickens to produce medicinal proteins in their eggs. 1 This immediately stood out to us as a potential, incredible solution. Although there have been 20 years of labs, companies, and startups trying to do this, what we saw is that it's been very inefficient, very hard to engineer chickens, but now there are these new technologies that would increase the editing efficiency by 100 or 1,000 times. So, that kind of all fell into place. Precision Engineering of Chickens and Hijacking Their Native Machinery Even with improved genetic engineering tools, how hard is it to edit chickens? Levin: It's a startup, so everything's hard. Plus, it's biology, so everything goes wrong and takes longer than it should. But the incredible thing is that we moved into our lab a little over a year ago, and we now have five genetically engineered lines of chickens. And that's not to say it was easy. We had to recruit the world's best genome engineers to do this work, but we are moving very quickly and having a very high success rate. That is in part because we are building on the shoulders of giants and 30 years of research that has solved what not to do. We have strong advisors, partners, and collaborators, and all of the academic teams and scientists, who have been working on this technology of genetically engineering chickens for 25 years. What genes are you engineering in chickens? Levin: The basic technique is to harness the native genetic architecture that drives protein production in the egg. Half the protein in the egg white is ovalbumin, so we simply take a gene that codes for our medicine, and we insert it into the ovalbumin locus. We're harnessing the native machinery for producing proteins in the eggs.
